title: Fallacies in Arguments
short: Spot common fallacies in real writing, by the Logic Ladder’s names: attacking the person, straw man, false dilemma, hasty generalization, slippery slope and others.
trouble: Learners call any argument they disagree with a fallacy. A fallacy is a flaw in the reasoning, not a conclusion you dislike.

blocks.html: On the Logic Ladder you met fallacies one at a time: attacking the person, the straw man, the false dilemma and hasty generalization, among others. In real writing they hide inside ordinary paragraphs. Spotting them is part of reading an argument well, and of rebutting fairly.

head: Fallacy (Logic Ladder name)
The flaw
In a letter to the editor
rows: Attacking the Person
rejects a claim by attacking who made it
“Of course she wants a skate park; she’s a teenager.”
Straw Man
swaps the real view for a weaker one
“Tree supporters want the town to spend every dollar on leaves.”
False Dilemma
offers two options when there are more
“Either we close the pool or we raise taxes.”
Hasty Generalization
leaps from too few cases
“Two kids skipped class, so students don’t care about school.”
Slippery Slope
predicts a chain of results without reasons for each link
“Allow phones at lunch, and soon no one will learn anything.”
Red Herring
changes the subject
“Why worry about the library’s hours when the roads have potholes?”
Appeal to the People
true or good because many believe or do it
“Everyone in town already supports it.”
False Cause
one thing came first, so it caused the other
“The team lost after the new coach came, so she is the problem.”
blocks.cap: Eight common fallacies, by the Logic Ladder’s names.

blocks.html: A fallacy is a flaw in the reasoning, not a conclusion you dislike. Name the flaw by what the faulty step does, then answer it by bringing the argument back to the real issue.

Fallacies persuade because they look like reasons. Naming them in your own drafts keeps you honest, and naming them in others’ writing (politely) shows readers exactly where an argument breaks, which is stronger than simply disagreeing.

blocks.title: Name it, then answer it
blocks.q: “If the school lets students choose one elective, next they’ll want to choose all their classes, and soon there will be no required subjects at all.”
steps: The writer predicts a chain: one elective → all classes → no requirements.
No reason is given for why each step would follow. That is a slippery slope.
A fair answer: “The proposal is for one elective. If later proposals go further, they can be judged on their own merits.”
blocks.a: Slippery slope; answer it by returning to the actual proposal.

blocks.title: Not every flaw you see is a fallacy
blocks.q: “Nearly all the veterinarians in the state survey recommend a yearly checkup for dogs, so you should probably take yours in.” A reader objects: “Appeal to authority!” Is it?
steps: The Logic Ladder separates fair and unfair appeals to authority.
Here the experts speak about their own field, and the claim is qualified (“probably”).
That is a reasonable appeal, not a fallacy.
blocks.a: No: citing experts in their own field, where they agree, is fair.

blocks.html: Calling any argument you disagree with a fallacy. An argument can reach a conclusion you dislike by perfectly good reasoning, and a fallacy can be used for a conclusion you like. Check: point to the exact step that goes wrong and name what it does. If you can’t, it may be a disagreement, not a fallacy. The Logic Ladder’s Good Reasoning That Looks Like a Fallacy shows the fair cousins of each fallacy.

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: The pool loses about \$20,000 a year, according to the parks report.
The people who want it closed have never cared about kids anyway.
A smaller summer schedule would cut the loss by half.
Either we keep the pool open every day or we lose it forever.

blocks.why: Sentence 2 attacks the people (attacking the person); sentence 4 offers only two options (false dilemma).
